cases.proof: Each iteration discards at least half of the remaining [lo, hi] range, so the range size shrinks geometrically from n to 0, giving O(log n) iterations with O(1) work each. Only scalar index variables are used.
cases.assumptions: a is sorted ascending; n = a.size().

cases.proof: The half-open range [lo, hi) halves in size on every iteration since mid strictly separates lo from hi (lo <= mid < hi), so the loop runs O(log n) times with O(1) work per iteration.
cases.assumptions: a is sorted ascending; n = a.size().

cases.proof: Same structural argument as lower_bound: the half-open range [lo, hi) strictly shrinks by roughly half on every iteration, giving O(log n) iterations of O(1) work each.
cases.assumptions: a is sorted ascending; n = a.size().

cases.proof: Even though a match continues the search (hi = mid - 1) instead of returning immediately, [lo, hi] still shrinks by at least half every iteration in all three branches, giving O(log n) total iterations.
cases.assumptions: a is sorted ascending (duplicates allowed); n = a.size().

cases.proof: Symmetric to first-occurrence: every branch strictly shrinks [lo, hi] by at least half, giving O(log n) total iterations regardless of how many duplicate values are present.
cases.assumptions: a is sorted ascending (duplicates allowed); n = a.size().

cases.proof: Each recursive call halves the [lo, hi] range and makes exactly one further recursive call, giving a recurrence T(n) = T(n/2) + O(1), which solves to O(log n) time. Since C++ does not guarantee tail-call elimination, the recursion depth of O(log n) frames is counted as O(log n) auxiliary stack space.
cases.assumptions: a is sorted ascending; called initially with lo=0, hi=(int)a.size()-1; n = a.size().

cases.proof: A single forward pass over weights performs O(1) work per element, giving O(n) time; only scalar counters are used.
cases.assumptions: n = weights.size(); this is the feasibility predicate used inside binarySearchOnAnswerMinShipCapacity.

cases.proof: The search range [lo, hi] over candidate capacities shrinks by half each iteration, giving O(log S) iterations where S = hi - lo is the initial capacity range (bounded by the total weight sum). Each iteration calls canShipWithinDays, which costs O(n), so total time is O(n log S).
cases.assumptions: n = weights.size(); S = sum(weights) - max(weights), the initial search range size.

cases.proof: The [lo, hi) range halves each iteration as in a standard lower_bound search, giving O(log n) calls to isTrue. Estimated because isTrue is a std::function whose own per-call cost is assumed O(1) here (a monotonic property check); if it hides non-constant work the true bound would scale accordingly.
cases.assumptions: isTrue is monotonic (false...false true...true) over [0, n) and assumed O(1) per call; n is the given search space size.

cases.proof: In the true branch, lo is set to mid instead of mid + 1. When lo and hi are adjacent (hi = lo + 1), mid = lo, so this update leaves lo unchanged, and the loop condition lo < hi remains true indefinitely: the range never shrinks. No finite iteration bound can be proven from this code.
cases.assumptions: This is intentionally a malformed update rule; termination is not guaranteed for all inputs, so no time bound can be assigned.

cases.proof: In the false branch, lo is set to mid rather than mid + 1. Since mid = lo + (hi-lo)/2 rounds toward lo, when hi = lo + 1 this yields mid = lo, so lo stays unchanged and lo < hi remains true forever. No finite iteration bound can be proven from this code.
cases.assumptions: This is intentionally a malformed update rule; termination is not guaranteed for all inputs, so no time bound can be assigned.

cases.proof: The for-loop bound is the literal 100, not derived from any runtime input symbol, so the function always performs exactly 100 predicate evaluations regardless of the input range or predicate. This is constant work from the analyzer's perspective (excluding the unknown internal cost of predicate itself).
cases.assumptions: predicate is assumed O(1) per call; iteration count is a hardcoded literal, not related to a desired precision input symbol.

cases.proof: The doubling loop runs O(log n) times to find a bounding range (bound at most doubles past n). The subsequent binary search operates on a range of size at most 'bound', which is O(n) but itself found in O(log n) steps, and the binary search over it costs O(log(bound)) = O(log n). Total is O(log n) + O(log n) = O(log n).
cases.assumptions: a is sorted ascending; n = a.size().

cases.proof: Every iteration determines which half of [lo, hi] is properly sorted in O(1) and discards at least half the range based on that check, so the range shrinks geometrically, giving O(log n) iterations with O(1) work each.
cases.assumptions: a is a sorted array rotated at an unknown pivot, with distinct elements; n = a.size().

cases.proof: The [lo, hi] range still halves each iteration, giving O(log n) calls to compare; however compare is an externally supplied function pointer whose internal complexity is unknown at this call site, so the total time (number of calls times unknown per-call cost) cannot be reduced to a concrete bound.
cases.assumptions: Number of comparator calls is O(log n), but overall time is Unknown due to the unresolved per-call cost of compare.

cases.proof: Structurally identical to the general recursive case: each call halves the range and makes one recursive call, giving O(log n) calls total. Space is reported as O(log n) for the call stack because the C++ standard does not guarantee tail-call optimization even for calls in tail position.
cases.assumptions: a is sorted ascending; called initially with lo=0, hi=(int)a.size()-1; n = a.size(); worst-case space assumes no compiler tail-call elimination.

cases.proof: The [lo, hi] range halves each iteration, so guess is called O(log n) times; however guess is an opaque externally supplied function (e.g., could perform arbitrary work per call) whose cost is not visible here, so the total time cannot be pinned to a concrete bound without knowing guess's implementation.
cases.assumptions: Number of probes is O(log n), but overall time is Unknown due to the unresolved per-call cost of guess.

cases.proof: std::lower_bound and std::upper_bound on a vector's random-access iterators are each guaranteed O(log n) comparisons by the standard; std::distance on random-access iterators is O(1). Total time is O(log n).
cases.assumptions: a is sorted ascending; n = a.size().

cases.proof: The block-jump loop runs O(n / step) times where step = O(sqrt(n)), contributing O(sqrt(n)) steps; the final linear scan is bounded by the block size, also O(sqrt(n)). Total time is O(sqrt(n)).
cases.assumptions: a is sorted ascending; n = a.size(); step is chosen as floor(sqrt(n)) (minimum 1).

cases.proof: A single forward pass over a performs O(1) work per element, giving O(n) time; only scalar counters are used.
cases.assumptions: n = a.size(); this is the feasibility predicate used inside binarySearchOnAnswerMinMaxPartition.

cases.proof: The candidate-sum range [lo, hi] halves each iteration, giving O(log S) iterations where S is the initial range (sum(a) - max(a)). Each iteration calls canPartitionWithMaxSum, costing O(n), so total time is O(n log S).
cases.assumptions: n = a.size(); S = sum(a) - max(a), the initial search range size; 1 <= m <= n.

cases.proof: Explicit empty check handles n=0 in O(1). For n>=1 the loop follows the same halving structure as the classic binary search, giving O(log n) worst-case iterations (which degenerates to O(1) for n=1 but is reported using the general n-parameterized bound).
cases.assumptions: a is sorted ascending when non-empty; n = a.size().
